lines.text: If both an argument in favor of and an argument against a measure have been selected for publication in the Sample
Ballot & Official Voter Information Pamphlet, a typed rebuttal to the argument in favor of or the argument against the
measure may be submitted as outlined in this form.
The author(s) of the primary argument of the measure may prepare and submit a rebuttal argument or may authorize
in writing any other person or persons to prepare, submit or sign the rebuttal argument.
A rebuttal argument will not be accepted unless accompanied by this completed form, which shall contain the printed
name(s) and signature(s) of the person(s) submitting it or, if submitted on behalf of a bona fide association of citizens,
the name of the association and the printed name and signature of at least one of its principal officers. Please make
sure you are using proper format before submitting to the Elections Office.
Word count limit for Rebuttal Arguments = 250 words

Rebuttal to the Argument in Favor of Measure P
Don't let the group proposing this measure fool you. Voting for Measure P will NOT save
downtown, will NOT improve parking, and will NOT create affordable homes.
This small group prioritizes inefficient parking lots over the community's needs. They ignore
vacant storefronts. They ignore the young families, seniors, teachers, nurses, firefighters, city
staff, retail employees, and others who are priced out of Menlo Park.
Measure P will block affordable homes and convenient, modern parking downtown. Measure P
risks losing local control city-wide because, despite what the proponents say, the city's annual
report shows that the downtown sites are essential to the city's plan for affordable homes.
Measure P ignores reality and the need to address housing costs in Menlo Park. Unnecessary
barriers will only worsen our affordability crisis. Our community cannot afford Measure P.
Measure P includes a poison pill: if anyone sues over this measure, only the three people who
put it on the ballot — not voters, not City Council — get to make the final decision about
defending it. But Menlo Park taxpayers pay the legal fees.
Measure P supporters say building housing downtown will hurt business. This is FALSE. As we
have seen in neighboring communities, improving parking and adding housing means more
Measure P would interfere with the City's decision-making process related to City-owned
downtown parking lot properties, including improvements.
Measure P is bad policy that makes our community more expensive and less accessible.
Join us, Congressman Sam Liccardo, and Habitat for Humanity in voting NO on Measure P to
